blocks.text: Know that this figure is irony. For who is there who does not know that the labour of the bee is honey? Further, it is truly said that honey is used πρὸς ὑγίειαν [pros hygieian], for health. For so the ancients hold. Hippocrates, chapter 50 of On Affections: Μέλι, ξὺν ἑτέροις ἐσθιόμενον, καὶ τρέφει, καὶ εὔχροιαν παρέχει [Meli, xyn heterois esthiomenon, kai trephei, kai euchroian parechei]; Honey, eaten with other things, both nourishes and gives a good colour. And in chapter 54: Οἶνος καὶ μέλι κάλλιστα κέκριται ἐν ἀνθρώποισι, ἢν πρὸς φύσιν καὶ ὑγιαίνουσι, καὶ ἀσθενέουσι, σὺν καιρῷ, καὶ μετριότητι, προσφέρονται [Oinos kai meli kallista kekritai en anthrōpoisi, ēn pros physin kai hygiainousi, kai astheneousi, syn kairō, kai metriotēti, prospherontai]; Wine and honey have been judged best for human beings, if they are given in accordance with nature to both the healthy and the weak, at the right time and in moderation. Diophanes, book 15 of the Geoponica: Οὐ μόνον ἡδὺ τοῖς χρωμένοις, ἀλλὰ καὶ μακροβίους ποιεῖ· οἱ οὖν γήρᾳ μέλιτι μετὰ ἄρτου μόνου τρεφόμενοι, ἐπὶ πλεῖστον βιοῦσι· καὶ τὰς αἰσθήσεις δὲ διαφυλάττει πάσας ἐῤῥωμένας [Ou monon hēdy tois chrōmenois, alla kai makrobious poiei; hoi oun gēra meliti meta artou monou trephomenoi, epi pleiston biousi; kai tas aisthēseis de diaphylattei pasas errōmenas]. Honey is not only pleasant to those who use it, but also makes them long-lived. So those who in old age eat honey with bread alone live a long time; and that food keeps the senses vigorous. Accordingly, Λύκος πολυχρονίους φησὶν εἶναι τοὺς Κυρνίους, διὰ τὸ μέλιτι ἀεὶ χρῆσθαι [Lykos polychronious phēsin einai tous Kyrnious, dia to meliti aei chrēsthai]: Lycus reports that the Corsicans are long-lived, because they always use honey. So Athenaeus, book 2, chapter 7. And in the same place: Τῶν Πυθαγορικῶν τροφὴ ἄρτος μετὰ μέλιτος, ὥς φησι Ἀριστόξενος, τοὺς προσφερομένους αὐτὰ ἀεὶ ἐπ᾽ ἀρίστῳ λέγων ἀνόσως διατελεῖν [Tōn Pythagorikōn trophē artos meta melitos, hōs phēsi Aristoxenos, tous prospheromenous auta aei ep' aristō legōn anosōs diatelein]. Aristoxenus writes that the food of the Pythagoreans was bread with honey, adding that those who always take these at their midday meal live free of disease. They seem to have learned this from their teacher, Pythagoras, of whom Eustathius on Iliad λ᾽ [l']: Ὡς δὲ καὶ τρόφιμον τὸ μέλι Πυθαγορᾶς μαρτυρεῖ, ὃς, εὐτελέστατα διαβιοὺς, πολλάκις μέλιτι μόνῳ ἠρκεῖτο [Hōs de kai trophimon to meli Pythagoras martyrei, hos, eutelestata diabious, pollakis meliti monō ērkeito]. Pythagoras also testifies that honey can nourish; living very frugally, he was mostly content with honey alone. To the same effect is the old proverb about Glaucus, Γλαῦκος πινὼν μέλι ἀνέστη [Glaukos pinōn meli anestē]: Glaucus, having drunk honey, came back to life; that is, if I grasp the meaning of the Paroemiographer, he recovered from a grave illness. And Athenaeus writes of Democritus that, when he had already been given up for dead, διαζῆσαι ἡμέρας ἱκανὰς, τῇ ἀπὸ τοῦ μέλιτος ἀναφορᾷ μόνῃ τρεφόμενον [diazēsai hēmeras hikanas, tē apo tou melitos anaphora monē trephomenon], he prolonged his life for some days, nourished only by the smell of honey. For, as follows in the same place, he took the greatest delight in the use of honey. So Πρὸς τὸν πυθόμενον, Πῶς ἂν ὑγιῶς τις διάγοι; ἔφη, Εἰ τὰ μὲν ἐντὸς μέλιτι βρέχοι, τὰ δὲ ἐκτὸς ἐλαίῳ [Pros ton pythomenon, Pōs an hygiōs tis diagoi? ephē, Ei ta men entos meliti brechoi, ta de ektos elaiō]; [col. 515] to one who asked how a person might live his life in health, he replied: if the inner parts of the body were moistened with honey, the outer with oil. Not much differently Diophanes: Δημόκριτος δὲ, ἐρωτηθεὶς, Πῶς ἂν ἄνοσοι καὶ μακραίωνες γίγνοιντο οἱ ἄνθρωποι; εἶπεν, Εἰ τὰ μὲν ἔξωθεν ἐλαίῳ τοῦ σώματος, τὰ δὲ ἔνδοθεν μέλιτι [Dēmokritos de, erōtētheis, Pōs an anosoi kai makraiōnes gignointo hoi anthrōpoi? eipen, Ei ta men exōthen elaiō tou sōmatos, ta de endothen meliti] [III, 371] χρήσαιντο [chrēsainto]. For this I would prefer χρίσαιντο [chrisainto]. From the same source is drawn the saying of Pollio, of which Pliny, book 22, chapter 24: Many have sustained a long old age on the nourishment of mead alone, with no other food at all, as in the famous example of Pollio Romulus. When he was past his hundredth year, the Divine Augustus, his guest, asked him by what means above all he had preserved that vigour of mind and body. And he replied: within by mead, without by oil. Mulsum [mead], that is, τῷ οἰνομέλιτι [tō oinomeliti]. It is clear, then, that honey is rightly placed among the dishes of kings and great men. This is easily proved by examples taken from Scripture. Thus honey is sent as a choice gift to Joseph, viceroy of Egypt, Gen. XLIII, 11. and to King David, when he was in the town of Mahanaim, neighbouring nobles offered honey, 2 Sam. XVII, 29. Solomon too speaks thus, Cant. V, 1. I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey. Not to mention Jonathan, the king's son, whose eyes and strength were restored by eating honey, 1 Sam. XIV, 27. If we add profane sources to these, in Iliad λ΄ [l'], line 630, we shall find that Hecamede set before Nestor and Patroclus at a banquet μέλι χλωρὸν [meli chlōron], yellow honey, or fresh honey. And in Odyssey υ΄ [y'], line 69, that Venus nourished the daughters of Pandarus τυρῷ, καὶ μέλιτι γλυκερῷ [tyrō, kai meliti glykerō], with cheese and sweet honey. So Suetonius on Nero, chapter 27: He also imposed dinners on his friends, of which one cost four million sesterces for the honeyed dishes; that is, one hundred thousand gold pieces, by Budé's reckoning. But the word mellita [honeyed dishes], which the common editions have, the most learned Casaubon changed into mitellita, because the oldest manuscripts read so. Yet he candidly admits that he does not know what mitellita are. Today, since the invention of sugar, no one will be surprised that honey has lost much of its value. 7. It is added that the bee is ποθεινὴν καὶ ἐπίδοξον [potheinēn kai epidoxon], beloved and renowned, among all. For honey is produced everywhere, as Pliny notes, book 22, chapter 23, and it is valued everywhere, from farthest Scythia to the Africans and Ethiopians. Augustine, or whoever the author is, in Sermon 15 To the Brothers in the Desert, writes that the philosopher Aristodemus toiled for many years in investigating the nature of the bee. But for Aristodemus I would gladly write Aristomachus, of whom Pliny, book 11, chapter 9: Let no one wonder that men have been captivated by love of them (the bees), that Aristomachus of Soli did nothing else for fifty-eight years, while Philiscus of Thasos, who kept bees in the wilderness, was surnamed Agrius [the Wild]. 8. Finally, the conclusion is this: Although (the bee) is weak in strength, τὴν σοφίαν τιμήσασα προήχθη [tēn sophian timēsasa proēchthē], because she honoured wisdom (that is, through the pursuit of wisdom) she has been advanced. That is, as prudence is ascribed to the serpent, so the pursuit of wisdom is ascribed to the bee καταχρηστικῶς [katachrēstikōs], since she does by natural instinct what, if human beings did it, would rightly enrol them in the catalogue of the wise. By this καταχρήσει [katachrēsei] not a few write that the bee is wise. Thus Lucian in the Halcyon calls the bee σοφὴν θείου μέλιτος ἐργάτιν [sophēn theiou melitos ergatin], the wise maker of divine honey. And Plutarch, Περὶ φιλοστοργίας [Peri philostorgias]: Τὴν μέλιτταν ἡμεῖς σοφὴν καλοῦμεν, καὶ νομίζομεν, ξανθὸν μέλι μηδομένην [Tēn melittan hēmeis sophēn kaloumen, kai nomizomen, xanthon meli mēdomenēn]; We call and consider the bee wise [III, 372] because she produces yellow honey.
